definition: DisCoCat (Categorical Compositional Distributional) is a mathematical framework for natural language processing which uses category theory to unify distributional semantics with the principle of compositionality.
details: The grammatical derivations in a categorial grammar (usually a pregroup grammar) are interpreted as linear maps acting on the tensor product of word vectors to produce the meaning of a sentence or a piece of text. String diagrams are used to visualise information flow and reason about natural language semantics.

explainer.lead: DisCoCat is a way to build the meaning of a sentence from the meanings of its words while respecting its grammar. It matters because word order and grammatical roles can be represented explicitly rather than treating a sentence as an unstructured collection of words.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sentence meaning as a construction made from word blocks, with grammar acting as the instructions for fitting them together. DisCoCat turns the blocks into numbers and the instructions into mathematical operations, so the whole sentence gets its own numerical meaning. It can also draw the connections as a diagram to show how information travels between words.
tiers.practitioner: A DisCoCat pipeline starts with word vectors and a grammatical derivation, usually from a pregroup grammar. The derivation determines linear maps applied to the tensor product of the vectors, producing a vector for the sentence or text. The main practical dependency is keeping the grammatical structure and the vector representation aligned; the framework does not itself prescribe how to obtain the word vectors.
tiers.paperLevel: For word vectors v_i in spaces V_i, a grammatical derivation is interpreted as a linear map f: V_1 ⊗ ... ⊗ V_n → S, and the sentence meaning is f(v_1 ⊗ ... ⊗ v_n). Categorial grammar, usually pregroup grammar, supplies the compositional structure, while string diagrams expose the information flow. The framework specifies composition rather than a particular method for learning word vectors.

explainer.example: For “Alice sees Bob,” take vectors for Alice, sees, and Bob. The grammatical derivation specifies how sees combines with its subject and object; interpreted as linear maps on their tensor product, it produces one vector representing the whole sentence.

explainer.intuition: Words supply distributional meanings as vectors, while grammar supplies the recipe for combining them. DisCoCat connects the two so that sentence meaning depends on both word content and grammatical structure.
howItWorks: Assign a vector to each word.
Derive the sentence's grammatical structure, usually with a pregroup grammar.
Form the tensor product of the word-vector spaces.
Interpret the derivation as linear maps acting on that product.
Use the resulting vector as the meaning of the sentence or text, with string diagrams showing the flow.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives distributional semantics an explicit account of compositionality: grammar controls how word meanings combine. Category theory and string diagrams provide a common mathematical language for both the calculation and its visualisation.
misconceptions: It is not just averaging word vectors; grammatical derivations determine the composition.
It is not a method for creating word vectors; it uses vectors supplied by distributional semantics.
String diagrams are not an extra meaning system; they visualise and support reasoning about the same structure.
